title: CRUD Operations with ADO.NET
description: Implement Create, Read, Update, and Delete operations using SqlCommand and ExecuteNonQuery.

data.text: CRUD stands for **Create, Read, Update, and Delete** — the four fundamental operations for persistent data. In ADO.NET, `SqlCommand` handles all four through its execution methods: `ExecuteReader()` for reads, and `ExecuteNonQuery()` for inserts, updates, and deletes.
The `SqlCommand` class provides three main methods for executing SQL against the database. Choosing the right one depends on what your query returns.

rows: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or DDL statements
Queries that return a single value

data.text: To insert a new record, write an INSERT statement and execute it with `ExecuteNonQuery()`. The method returns the number of rows affected, which should be 1 for a successful insert.

data.title: Insert a New Inventory Item
data.content: Add a new product to the Inventory table.

data.title: Always use parameters
data.text: Never concatenate user input into SQL strings. Always use parameterized queries (SqlParameter) to prevent SQL injection attacks. The example above uses parameters correctly.
Reading data uses `ExecuteReader()` to get a `SqlDataReader`. You can also use `ExecuteScalar()` when you need a single aggregate value, such as a count or sum.

data.title: Get Total Inventory Count with ExecuteScalar
data.content: Retrieve a single aggregate value efficiently.

data.text: For reading multiple rows, use `ExecuteReader()` as shown in the previous lesson. You can also combine a read with an update in a single round-trip by returning the identity of the newly inserted row.

data.title: Get Inserted Identity Value
data.content: Retrieve the auto-generated Id after inserting a row.

data.text: Updating records follows the same pattern as inserting. Use an UPDATE statement with a WHERE clause to target specific rows. Always include a WHERE clause; omitting it updates every row in the table.

data.title: Update an Inventory Item
data.content: Change the price and quantity of an existing product.

data.text: Deleting records is straightforward but dangerous without a WHERE clause. Always verify the row exists and confirm the intent before deleting. A soft-delete pattern (setting an IsDeleted flag) is often safer in production applications.

data.title: Delete an Inventory Item
data.content: Remove a product by its Id.

data.text: A typical ADO.NET controller follows a consistent pattern: open a connection, create a command with parameters, execute, and close. The using statement handles disposal automatically.

data.title: CRUD Controller Skeleton
data.content: A complete controller outline showing all four operations.

items.text: INSERT uses parameters for all user-supplied values.
SELECT retrieves all columns needed by the view.
items.hint: Use SELECT * or list columns explicitly.

items.text: UPDATE includes a WHERE clause targeting the primary key.
DELETE uses a WHERE clause and targets the primary key.
items.hint: Never omit the WHERE clause in DELETE statements.

items.text: All connections are wrapped in using statements.
items.hint: Ensures proper disposal even if an exception occurs.

data.title: Exercise: Build a Full CRUD Controller
data.description: Create a complete InventoryController with all four operations.
steps: Create an InventoryController with Index, Create, Edit, and Delete actions.
Implement the Index action to read all Inventory records using SqlDataReader.
Implement the Create GET and POST actions to insert a new Inventory item.
Implement the Edit GET and POST actions to update an existing item.
Implement the Delete action to remove an item by Id.
Create simple Razor views for each action.
Test each operation by running the application.
data.expectedOutcome: A working CRUD interface for the Inventory table using only ADO.NET, no ORM.
